title: Respect — beliau, titles and asking permission
goal: Speak to and about people above you the way Indonesians expect: *beliau* instead of *dia*, *Bapak* and *Ibu* instead of “you”, *berkenan* and *mohon izin* instead of plain requests — and apologise properly to an elder when you get it wrong.
bekal: refer to a respected person as *beliau* and address them as *Bapak/Ibu* without ever saying *kamu* or *Anda*
ask permission and invite a superior with *mohon izin*, *berkenan* and *kalau jadwal memungkinkan*
apologise and excuse yourself in a Javanese village with *nuwun sewu*, *mohon maaf* and *matur nuwun*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di kantor Bupati
dialogs.intro: A Thursday in late May. Pak Harun and Sarah have an appointment with the Bupati, the head of Magelang Regency, to invite him to the village festival. Bu Sinta from the protocol office meets them in the waiting room.

lines.speaker: Sinta:
lines.text: Selamat pagi, Bapak, Ibu. Ada yang bisa kami bantu?

lines.literal: safe morning, Sir, Madam. exist which can we help?

lines.text: Selamat pagi, Bu. Saya Harun, Kepala Desa Sumberwangi. Kami sudah ada janji dengan Bapak Bupati pukul sepuluh.
lines.id: Good morning. I'm Harun, head of Sumberwangi village. We have an appointment with the Regent at ten.

notes: **Beliau** is “he” or “she” for someone you respect: a boss, an official, a teacher, an older relative, the dead. It is never used for yourself or for someone present whom you are addressing. Using *dia* for the Bupati in his own office would sound startlingly rude.

**Bapak and Ibu as “you”.** In polite Indonesian you do not say *Anda* to a superior, and never *kamu*: you say *Bapak* or *Ibu*, in the third person. *Terima kasih atas waktu yang Bapak berikan* is literally “thanks for the time that Sir gave”. The same trick works with *Mbak*, *Mas* and titles like *Dokter*.

**Berkenan** — “to be pleased to, to deign to” — is how you ask a superior to do something without seeming to give an order. *Bapak berkenan menunggu?* is far softer than *Bisa tunggu?*, and *Kami berharap Bapak berkenan membuka…* is the standard invitation to officials.

**Mohon izin** — “I beg permission” — comes from military and civil-service culture and is now everywhere in formal settings: before speaking, before leaving, before taking a photo, even before disagreeing. Sarah uses it to enter the conversation.

**Pendapa** (spoken *pendopo*) is the open-sided Javanese pavilion at the front of a regent's residence or a traditional house, used for receptions and meetings. Regency offices in Central Java often have one.

**Kalau jadwal saya memungkinkan, saya usahakan** — “if my schedule allows, I'll try”. This is a real maybe, not a no, but it is also not a yes. The follow-up (*nanti staf saya yang mengabari*) is where the answer will come from, so Sarah should keep in touch with Bu Sinta.

grammars.title: The respect ladder: pronouns
body: Indonesian has more than one word for “he” and “you”, and choosing between them is choosing a relationship. Move one step up whenever you are not sure.
after: *Kami* rather than *kita* is itself a form of respect when you speak to officials: it keeps a polite distance between your group and theirs.
⚠️ *Anda* looks polite in the textbook but can feel cold or even confrontational face to face with an older person. Use it on forms and in advertisements; to people, use a title.

grammars.title: Honorific verbs
body: For some everyday actions Indonesian keeps a special verb for people you respect, in the same spirit as English “passed away” for “died”. Use the right-hand column about an official, an elder or a host.
after: *Menghadap* literally means “to face”: *Saya ingin menghadap Bapak Kepala Dinas* is how you ask for an audience with a department head.
*Mati* is only used for animals, plants, machines and enemies. For people it is *meninggal* at minimum, and *wafat* or *berpulang* for someone honoured.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Minta maaf kepada Mbah Wiryo
dialogs.intro: The following week. A group of Sarah's visitors walked into the village cemetery and photographed a family praying at their ancestors' graves without asking. Sarah goes to see Mbah Wiryo, the oldest and most respected man in the village, in the late afternoon.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nuwun sewu, Mbah. Mohon maaf mengganggu sore-sore begini.
lines.id: Excuse me, Mbah. I'm sorry to disturb you so late in the afternoon.
lines.literal: excuse-me, grandfather. beg forgiveness disturb afternoon-afternoon like-this.

lines.text: Monggo, monggo, Nduk. Silakan duduk. Ada apa, kok kelihatan susah?

lines.text: Oh, itu. Iya, ada warga yang tersinggung. Makam itu tempat leluhur, Nduk.

lines.speaker: Wiryo:
lines.text: Nanti saya antar ke rumah Pak Sastro. Sampaikan baik-baik, orang sini tidak pendendam.

lines.text: Matur nuwun, Mbah. Mulai minggu depan kami pasang papan “Mohon izin sebelum memotret”.

notes: **Nuwun sewu** is Javanese for “excuse me” (literally “a thousand pardons”) and is said when entering, passing in front of someone, or starting a delicate subject. From a foreigner it is disarming and much appreciated. *Matur nuwun* is Javanese “thank you”; *monggo* is “please, go ahead, come in”.

**Mbah** is grandparent — any very old man or woman in Central and East Java can be addressed this way. **Nduk** (from *genduk*) is how elders call a girl or young woman affectionately; the male equivalent is *Le* (from *thole*).

**Sore-sore begini** — reduplication plus *begini* adds “at this hour, of all times”: an apology for the timing built into the phrase. *Pagi-pagi* (bright and early) and *malam-malam* (so late at night) work the same way.

**Berziarah** means visiting graves to pray and tidy them — families do it on Thursday afternoons, before Ramadan and after Lebaran; the big communal Javanese version before Ramadan is *nyadran*. *Sedang berziarah* shows why the photos hurt: it was a private family moment, not a show.

**Wong** in Javanese-flavoured Indonesian is a particle meaning “after all, well, you see”: *Wong dia belum tahu* — “well, he didn't know, did he”. It excuses and explains at the same time. (As a noun *wong* means “person” in Javanese.)

**Diminum dulu tehnya** — a host's offer in the passive: “let the tea be drunk first”. It is the most typical way to say “please have your drink” in Java. *Keburu dingin* means “(it'll) get cold before you know it”; *keburu* = “before there is time”.

grammars.title: The apology ladder
body: Indonesian apologies scale up with the seriousness of the offence and the status of the person. Sarah, rightly, climbs quite high.

head: Expression
Use
Register
rows: a small slip with a friend
excuse me, in Java; to elders

after: The strongest apology is not a stronger phrase but a visit in person, as Sarah does. Sending a WhatsApp message for something like this would make it worse.
*Seharusnya saya…* (“I should have…”) turns an apology into an acknowledgement that you understand the rule, which is what an elder wants to hear.

blocks.text: The safest rule: address people by title, refer to them by title, and let *beliau* do the rest. Here is a map of the people Sarah deals with every week.

head: Person
To their face
Talking about them
rows: an old man in the village
a woman of your age at work
a waiter, driver or shop assistant

blocks.text: *Masnya* and *mbaknya* — “the guy”, “the lady” — are the natural, friendly way to refer to a young stranger: *Tanya mbaknya saja* (just ask the lady there).
Much Indonesian politeness is not in the words at all but in asking before you act. The phrases are short; the habit is what counts.

head: Situation
What to say
What to do
rows: bend slightly, right arm down in front
wait to hear *Monggo!* before going in
shake hands with the most senior first
wait for a nod, especially at ceremonies
take a little anyway if you can

blocks.title: Body language that speaks for you
items: Give and receive with the right hand, or both hands for something important. The left hand alone can look disrespectful.
Point with the thumb of the right hand, not the index finger.
Do not touch an adult's head, and take your shoes off where you see others' shoes at the door.
*Salim* — touching an elder's hand to your forehead or nose — is for children and younger family members; as a guest, a gentle handshake with a slight nod is right.
